items.prompt: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about what orangutans eat?

options.text: Orangutans eat mainly fruit, but they also eat leaves, bark and insects.
Orangutans live in Borneo and Sumatra.
options.why: This sentence is about where they live.

options.text: My favourite animal at the zoo is the elephant.
options.why: This is not about orangutans.
This is about their age, not their food.

hints: A topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about.
The paragraph is about food.
Find the sentence that mentions what orangutans eat.
items.explanation: A topic sentence introduces the main idea. This one tells the reader that the paragraph is about what orangutans eat.

items.prompt: Choose a connective from the box to fill the gap. Box: However, Therefore, For example. Many people enjoy Car Free Day. ___, some shop owners are unhappy about it.
hints: Read both sentences. Do they agree or contrast?
You need a connective that shows a different side.
Try each connective in the gap and read the two sentences aloud.
items.explanation: However shows a contrast: many people enjoy it, but some shop owners are unhappy.

items.prompt: Match each connective to its job.
pairs: to show something happening at the same time
hints: Connectives link ideas between sentences and paragraphs.
Think of a sentence that could follow each connective.
Start with For example. What usually comes after it?
items.explanation: However contrasts, as a result shows an effect, for example gives an example and meanwhile shows the same time. Finally introduces the last point, and in addition adds another one.

items.prompt: Put the sentences in order to make a clear paragraph.
items: Sea turtles lay their eggs on sandy beaches.
First, the mother digs a deep hole with her back flippers.
Then she lays around a hundred eggs inside it.
After that, she covers the eggs with sand and returns to the sea.
About two months later, the baby turtles hatch and head for the waves.
hints: Look for the topic sentence that introduces the paragraph.
Then use the time connectives: first, then, after that, later.
Start with the sentence that does not begin with a time word.
items.explanation: The topic sentence comes first, then the time connectives First, Then, After that and About two months later put the steps in order.

items.prompt: Which sentence would best begin a new paragraph that moves the story to a different time?

options.why: This describes the parcel but does not move the time on.
This adds a detail. It does not show a change of time.

options.text: Also, the parcel had a label.
options.why: Also adds a detail. It does not show a change of time.

options.text: Three days later, the parcel finally arrived.

hints: New paragraphs often start when the time or place changes.
Look for a phrase that tells the reader when.
Find the sentence that starts with a time phrase.
items.explanation: Three days later tells the reader that time has passed, so it is a good way to start a new paragraph.

items.prompt: Read: Dewi gave Tara her book before she left. Why is this sentence unclear?

options.why: Gave and left are verbs.

options.text: We cannot tell whether her and she mean Dewi or Tara.

options.why: Punctuation is not the problem here.

options.text: Book should have a capital letter.
options.why: Book is a common noun, so it does not need one.

hints: Look at the pronouns her and she.
A pronoun should point clearly to one person.
Ask: whose book was it, and who left?
items.explanation: Her and she could mean either Dewi or Tara. Using a name instead of a pronoun would make the sentence clear.

items.prompt: Paragraph 1 explains why bees are important to farmers. Paragraph 2 describes the dangers bees face. Which sentence best links the two paragraphs?

options.text: Bees are insects with six legs.
options.why: This does not link the two ideas.

options.text: Despite their importance, bees face many dangers.

options.why: This does not link the two ideas.

options.text: In addition, bees are important to farmers.
options.why: This repeats the first paragraph and does not lead into the second.

hints: A good linking sentence looks back and looks forward.
It should mention the idea of paragraph 1 and introduce the idea of paragraph 2.
Find the sentence that mentions both importance and dangers.
items.explanation: Despite their importance looks back to paragraph 1, and bees face many dangers introduces paragraph 2.

items.prompt: Choose all the words and phrases that link ideas across a text.

options.why: Quickly tells us how something is done. It does not link ideas.
Beautiful is an adjective. It does not link ideas.

hints: Linking words connect one idea to another.
They can show results, contrasts or changes in time.
Check each word: does it tell us how two ideas are connected?
items.explanation: Consequently shows a result, on the other hand shows a contrast and later that evening shows a change in time.

items.prompt: Which sentence breaks the flow of this paragraph? (1) Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. (2) Some kinds grow almost a metre in a day. (3) My cousin plays the flute in a band. (4) Bamboo is used to build houses, furniture and even bicycles.

options.why: This is the topic sentence about bamboo.
This gives evidence for the topic sentence.
This adds more information about bamboo.

hints: Every sentence in a paragraph should be about the same topic.
The topic is given in sentence 1.
Check each sentence: is it about bamboo?
items.explanation: Sentence 3 is about a cousin playing the flute. Every other sentence is about bamboo, so sentence 3 breaks the flow.

items.prompt: Which connective would be wrong in the gap? The bridge was closed. ___, we had to take a longer route.

options.why: Therefore works here: it shows a result.
As a result works here: it shows a result.
Consequently works here: it shows a result.

hints: The second sentence is a result of the first.
Three of the connectives show a result. One shows a contrast.
Look for the connective that means in spite of this.
items.explanation: Nevertheless means in spite of this, so it signals a contrast. Taking a longer route is a result of the closed bridge, not a contrast.

items.prompt: Bayu was hungry. ___, he made a sandwich. He liked cheese. ___, he did not like tomato.
hints: A connective shows how two sentences are linked.
The first pair shows a result. The second pair shows a different side.
Hungry leads to making food. Liking cheese is different from disliking tomato.
items.explanation: Therefore shows a result of being hungry. However shows a contrast between liking cheese and disliking tomato.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be the best ending for a paragraph about recycling at school?

options.text: So, by recycling every day, our school can help to protect the environment.
The canteen sells rice and noodles.
options.why: This is a new idea and does not finish the paragraph.

options.text: Plastic bottles are made in many different shapes.
options.why: This adds a fact but does not conclude the paragraph.
This has nothing to do with recycling.

hints: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea.
It usually links back to the topic sentence.
Look for the sentence that is about recycling and finishes the point.
items.explanation: A concluding sentence ties the ideas together. This one returns to the topic of recycling and the purpose of the paragraph.

items.prompt: Put the sentences in order to make a clear paragraph.
items: Our school garden has become a busy place for learning.
At first, we cleared the weeds and dug the soil.
Next, we planted chillies, beans and spinach in neat rows.
Every morning, a different group waters the plants.
As a result, we now eat fresh vegetables at lunch.
hints: Look for the sentence that introduces the main idea.
Then follow the time words: at first, next, every morning.
As a result belongs near the end.
items.explanation: The topic sentence comes first. At first, Next and Every morning put the steps in order, and As a result gives the final effect.

items.prompt: Match each connective to the job it does.
pairs: shows what would happen if not
hints: Connectives tell the reader how ideas fit together.
Think of a sentence that could follow each one.
Start with In conclusion. Where in a text does it usually go?
items.explanation: Each connective has a clear job: adding, contrasting, summing up, showing sequence, showing similarity or showing a condition.

items.prompt: Sort the connectives by what they show.
hints: Ask what each connective does between two sentences.
Some add, some contrast, some give a result, some give time.
Start with Afterwards. Is it about time?
items.explanation: In addition and moreover add. On the other hand and despite this contrast. Consequently and because of this show a result. Afterwards and meanwhile show time.

items.prompt: Read: Rangga told Kofi that he had won the prize. Why is this sentence unclear, and how can it be fixed?

options.text: He could mean Rangga or Kofi. Use a name or rewrite it.
It has no verb. Add a verb.
options.why: The sentence has verbs. The problem is the pronoun.

options.text: It is too long. Cut it in half.
options.why: Length is not the problem here.

options.text: The word prize is wrong. Change it to gift.
options.why: The noun is fine. The unclear word is he.

hints: Look at the word he.
Who could it be pointing to?
Try replacing he with each name in turn.
items.explanation: He could refer to Rangga or to Kofi. Fix it by naming the person: Rangga told Kofi that Kofi had won the prize.

items.prompt: Paragraph 1 describes the problems caused by plastic bags. Paragraph 2 explains the solutions. Which sentence best begins paragraph 2?

options.text: Plastic bags are made from oil.
options.why: This repeats the problem and does not link to solutions.

options.text: Many children like to ride bicycles.
options.why: This does not link to the topic.

options.text: Fortunately, there are several simple ways to reduce the use of plastic bags.
In addition, plastic bags harm sea animals.
options.why: In addition adds another problem, but paragraph 2 is about solutions.

hints: The first sentence of a new paragraph links back and shows the new focus.
Paragraph 2 is about solutions.
Which sentence signals a change from problems to solutions?
items.explanation: Fortunately signals a change from problems to answers. It makes a smooth link between the paragraphs.

items.prompt: Write a connective that shows a result. Petrol has become more expensive. ___, many families now use bicycles.
hints: The second sentence is an effect of the first.
Use a connective, not a full sentence.
Try Therefore, As a result or Consequently.
items.explanation: Expensive petrol is the cause and more bicycles is the effect, so you need a connective that shows a result.

items.prompt: Build a sentence that shows two things happening at the same time. Use the cards.
items.answer: Meanwhile, the other team waited outside.
hints: One connective shows something happening at the same time.
The sentence starts with that connective and a comma.
The other team is the subject. The verb comes after it.
items.explanation: Meanwhile shows two events happening together. The comma comes after it, and the rest forms a normal sentence.

items.prompt: Put the sentences in order to make a cohesive paragraph about a lighthouse.
items: The old lighthouse on the cliff has guided ships for over a hundred years.
Its tall tower holds a powerful lamp that can be seen from far out at sea.
However, the lamp is now controlled by a computer, not by a keeper.
Consequently, the keeper’s cottage stands empty.
Visitors can still walk inside it and imagine life there long ago.
hints: The first sentence introduces the lighthouse.
Its in the second sentence points back to the lighthouse.
However introduces a change, and Consequently shows the result of that change.
items.explanation: The topic sentence comes first, then its describes the tower. However gives a contrast, Consequently shows the effect, and the last sentence adds a final detail.

items.prompt: Match each sentence from the paragraph about bats to its job.
hints: A topic sentence introduces the main idea.
Evidence gives a fact. Explanation says why the fact matters.
The last sentence usually sums up or gives advice.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces the idea, the second gives a fact, the third explains why it matters, and the last concludes.
pairs: One bat can eat thousands of insects in a night.
This helps farmers because fewer insects damage crops.
So, we should protect bats and their homes.

items.prompt: We went to the market. We bought mangoes. We bought rice. We went home. Choose all the edits that would improve the flow.

options.why: This makes the text vaguer and does not link the ideas.

options.text: Add Afterwards, before the last sentence.

options.why: This removes information and does not help the flow.

options.text: Change the third sentence to We also bought rice.

hints: Cohesion means the sentences link well.
Look for time words and words that add information.
Which edits show order and join the shopping ideas?
items.explanation: First and Afterwards show the order of events. Also links the two shopping sentences. The other edits do not help the flow.

items.prompt: Which order makes the best paragraph? A: As a result, the pond slowly turned green and smelly. B: Last summer, a farm near our village began pouring extra fertiliser into the stream. C: That is why villagers now ask farmers to use less fertiliser. D: The fertiliser washed into the pond and made the algae grow wildly.

options.why: As a result in A must come after the cause, which is D.
D uses the fertiliser before B has introduced it.
C is the conclusion and should come last.

hints: Find the sentence that introduces the topic. It has no linking word at the start.
As a result and That is why show effects, so they come after causes.
Put the cause (D) before the effect (A), and the conclusion last.
items.explanation: B introduces the cause, D shows what happened, A is the result and C is the conclusion.

items.prompt: Read: The museum is free. ___, it is very crowded at weekends. ___, we usually go on weekdays. Which pair of connectives fits?

options.why: The first gap needs a contrast and the second a result.
The first gap is not about time and the second is not a contrast.
Neither shows the right contrast or result.

hints: Work out how each pair of sentences is linked.
Free and crowded are a contrast. Crowded and weekdays is a result.
Fill the first gap with a contrast word.
items.explanation: The first link is a contrast (free but crowded), so However. The second link is a result (because it is crowded, we go on weekdays), so Therefore.

items.prompt: True or false: A topic sentence tells the reader the main idea of a paragraph.
hints: Which sentence sums up the paragraph?
It usually comes at the start.
Topic means main idea.
items.explanation: It usually comes first and the rest of the paragraph supports it.

items.prompt: True or false: A new paragraph is needed for every sentence.
hints: How many ideas does a paragraph have?
Think of grouping sentences.
One idea per paragraph.
items.explanation: A paragraph groups sentences about one idea, so a new paragraph begins with a new idea.

items.prompt: True or false: Connectives such as however and therefore link ideas between sentences.
hints: What do connecting words do?
However shows a difference.
They link ideas.
items.explanation: However shows contrast and therefore shows a result.

items.prompt: True or false: Pronouns such as it and they can link sentences by referring back to a noun.
hints: What does a pronoun stand for?
It points back.
It refers to a noun named earlier.
items.explanation: A pronoun refers to a noun already named, which helps the text flow.

items.prompt: True or false: The words firstly and secondly show contrast between ideas.
hints: Count in order.
Which words show a difference?
They show sequence.
items.explanation: Firstly and secondly show order. Contrast is shown by words such as however.

items.prompt: True or false: A new paragraph is usually started for a new topic, time or place.
hints: What changes in a story when the scene changes?
Think of a new setting.
Change calls for a new paragraph.
items.explanation: Paragraphs help the reader follow changes in a text.
